newsitem.title: USA: Camera prices have jumped but may head higher yet.
newsitem.headline: Camera prices have jumped but may head higher yet.

text.p: Prices have risen and the market is mature. But collecting cameras can still be fascinating -- and profitable -- since prices are likely to head higher still.

Don't expect to make a killing. Many of the oldest and rarest Leica, Nikon and Kodak cameras have already jumped in price. But there are opportunities if you know what you're looking for, dealers and collectors say.

"I won't say it's peaked but the rise in value over the next decade won't be the same as it was over the last 10 or 20 years," said John Craig, who got interested in the field while working in a camera store and majoring in history in college.
"The really rare stuff just went stratospheric," said Jay Tepper, a New Canaan, Conn., dealer. But there is "tremendous" potential for selected older models, he said.

Twenty years ago you could just collect cameras. Now most collectors specialise. There are Leica collectors and Voigtlander collectors. Some covet oddities such as miniature "spy" cameras or models with unusual colours or features.
New York dealer Allen Weiner, who specialises in fine antique cameras from 1840 to the turn of century, estimates that prices overall have been rising 5 percent to 10 percent a year.
"It's the kind of market that was never explosive. (Prices for old) watches exploded all of sudden, but the camera market has progressed more or less steadily," Weiner said.

The idea for the camera dates from the Greeks, when Aristotle referred to a "camera obscura", Latin for dark chamber, literally a dark box for viewing a scene. The first diagram of a camera is credited to Leonardo da Vinci in 1519.
Images were not recorded on light-sensitive material until more than 300 years later, when the Frenchmen Joseph Niepce and Louis Daguerre worked together until Niepce died in 1833.
The earliest cameras date from a few years later.

The first Kodak box cameras from the 1880s can be worth $3,000 or more for the rarest models, said Bob Coyle, a collector and photographer in Dubuque, Iowa. Those in the best condition will bring the most money.

Similar cameras from a decade later can fetch from $500 to $1,500, depending on model and condition, Coyle said. The cameras were made of polished wood with dovetail corners and featured shutters operated by a pull-string.
Other "string-set" shutter cameras range from $300 to a few thousand dollars apiece.
Sometimes one small feature can make an otherwise ordinary camera quite valuable.

Kodak made millions of folding "pocket" cameras earlier this century, most now worth $20 or so. But one model with a calf skin and satin bellows can bring $1,000 in good condition and an olive drab model with a khaki bellows can fetch several hundred dollars, according to Tepper, the Connecticut dealer.

The Kodak Super 620, the first camera with an automatic "electric eye" shutter and built-in light meter, has nearly doubled in price the last five years and can be worth $1,500 to $2,500, depending on condition, dealers said.
Tepper said one of his favourites is Kodak's Bantam Special, made around the same time as the Super 620. The Art Deco style Bantam, made in a dozen styles, never sold well in the 1930s and '40s.

"It's one of the nicest, if not THE nicest, looking metal-body camera that has ever been made," Tepper said. With black bodies striped in silver, the cameras can bring $200 to $400, compared with $100 to $125 just a few years back.
Nikons and Leicas, of course, are widely collected but prices are rich.

An original Nikon I from 1948 brings $25,000, about double five years ago, and several Leica models are worth that much, including the gold-plated Luxus and the 72, which takes 72 frames instead of the standard 36.
The more affordable Leica 3C, made before and after World War II, can be found for $150 to $500.
German-made Voigtlander cameras are also collectible.
A Bessa II, made with different lenses, can fetch from $500 to several times that, depending on condition and the lens. The most valuable is the Apo-Lanthar, said Iowa collector Coyle.
Other collectible cameras include Zeiss, Ansco and Argus.
Tepper said the best buys now are the earliest single lens reflex (SLR) models, such as the Nikon F, introduced in 1959, which can be found for $125 to $150.
"The F models are just starting to move up in price," he said. "I think the upside potential is tremendous."
He said the Minolta SR1 and Topcon and Canonflex SLRs may also be good buys.
One factor that has slowed the market recently is the weakness of the Japanese yen, since many collectors are in Japan. But that is probably temporary, dealers said.
Several noted that counterfeit Leicas are coming out of Russia and Eastern Europe. If you find what looks like a rare Leica and it seems inexpensive, check with a reputable dealer.
For more information, try CameraShopper, run by Tepper and his wife, which costs $20 for 10 issues. Write P.O. Box 1086, New Canaan, Conn. 06840 or call 203 972-5700.
The industry standard is McKeown's Price Guide to Antique and Classic Cameras from Centennial Photo. 715 689-2153.
